# Airworthiness of aircraft

> A healthy glider is a safe glider; learn to check your aircraft's “technical health” before every flight.
>
>
> In this chapter you will learn:
>
>
> * The difference between the **Certificate of Airworthiness** (CofA) and the **Airworthiness Review Certificate** (ARC), and what the law requires for you to fly with them in order.
> * The light aviation maintenance framework (Part-ML) from its legal side (the technical detail is covered in Book 8 — Aircraft General Knowledge, Airframe and Systems and Emergency Equipment).
> * What falls to you: the pre-flight inspection, checking the documents and reporting defects.

## The concept of airworthiness

Airworthiness is, in short, your aircraft's technical health. A glider is airworthy when it conforms to the design approved by the authority (its papers are in order) and is in a condition for safe operation, with no dangerous defects.

As the pilot, you are the last link in the safety chain. However well the aircraft is designed, if it is not properly maintained it stops being safe.

## Certificate of Airworthiness (CofA)

The **Certificate of Airworthiness** (CofA) is the document issued by the authority of the State of registry (AESA in Spain) to certify that the aircraft conforms to the approved design and is in a condition for safe operation.

The CofA of EASA aircraft is valid **indefinitely**: it does not expire, provided the aircraft is kept airworthy in accordance with its maintenance programme and nobody revokes it (@fig-01-cap02-cofa-example). To be valid, though, it must always be accompanied by a valid ARC. Without an ARC, the CofA is worthless.

![EASA Certificate of Airworthiness](imagenes/01-cap02-certificado-aeronavegabilidad.jpg){#fig-01-cap02-cofa-example}

## The annual “MOT”: the Airworthiness Review Certificate (ARC)

The **ARC** (**Airworthiness Review Certificate**) confirms that, at a given moment, someone reviewed the aircraft's documentation and physical condition and everything was in order.

It is valid for **one year**, so it has to be renewed or extended every year. In a controlled environment (managed by a CAMO or, in light aviation, by a CAO), the ARC can be extended twice in a row without a full physical review, that is, 1 year + 1 year + 1 year. In the third year, a thorough review with no excuses (@fig-01-cap02-arc-process). The technical regime behind the ARC (the maintenance programme, the minimum inspection programme and airworthiness directives) is covered in **Book 8 — Aircraft General Knowledge, Airframe and Systems and Emergency Equipment**, chapter 9; what matters here is its legal side: without a valid ARC you cannot fly.

::: {.callout-warning title="Safety"}
Never fly if the ARC has expired. It is illegal and, most importantly, it means nobody has officially certified in the last year that the aircraft is safe to fly. What is more, your insurer will very probably refuse cover if anything happens: most policies make it conditional on the aircraft being airworthy.
:::

![ARC life cycle and its extensions](imagenes/01-cap02-ciclo-arc.jpg){#fig-01-cap02-arc-process}

## Glider maintenance: Part-ML

From the legal point of view, all you need to retain is the framework: gliders are maintained under **Part-ML** (Annex Vb to Regulation (EU) No 1321/2014), a simplified set of rules for light aviation that rests on an **Aircraft Maintenance Programme (AMP)** and that, for certain simple tasks, allows the **pilot-owner** to sign off the maintenance personally. All of this in detail (how the AMP works, the minimum inspection programme, which tasks the pilot-owner may sign off and under what conditions, airworthiness directives (AD) and service bulletins (SB)) belongs to its natural subject, **Aircraft General Knowledge, Airframe and Systems and Emergency Equipment**: it is covered in **Book 8 — Aircraft General Knowledge, Airframe and Systems and Emergency Equipment**, chapter 9.

## Pilot responsibilities

You are not a mechanic, but you are the one ultimately responsible for accepting the aircraft for the flight. Three tasks are yours and nobody else's.

### 1. Pre-flight inspection

Before every flight you must carry out an external and internal inspection, following the checklist in the **Aircraft Flight Manual (AFM)**. It is a legal obligation, but above all it is common sense.

### 2. Checking the documentation

Before take-off, check that the mandatory documentation is on board and valid.
Under the sailplane operations rules (Part-SAO), this includes:

* **Aircraft documents**: CofA, ARC, Certificate of Registration, insurance, radio station licence.
* **Operational documents**: flight manual (AFM), checklists.
* **Pilot documents**: your licence (SPL) and your medical certificate.

### 3. Reporting defects

If you find something wrong during the pre-flight check or in flight, write it in the **technical log**. The next pilot will thank you.

::: {.callout-note title="Airmanship"}
See a chip in the gelcoat? It is not just cosmetic: if it affects the profile, it affects the flight. When in doubt, ask. Better a curious pilot than a pilot in trouble.
:::

::: {.postit}
**Chapter summary: airworthiness**

Airworthiness is your aircraft's health. To fly legally and safely:

* **CofA**: certifies that the aircraft conforms to the approved design and is in a condition for safe operation. It is issued by the State of registry (AESA in Spain) and does not expire if the aircraft is properly maintained.
* **ARC**: the annual “MOT”. It confirms that the aircraft has been reviewed and is fit. Check its expiry date before flying.
* **Part-ML**: the maintenance framework for gliders; it allows the pilot-owner to certify simple tasks. Its technical side (AMP, minimum inspection programme, AD/SB) is in **Book 8 — Aircraft General Knowledge, Airframe and Systems and Emergency Equipment**, chapter 9.
* **Your part**: carry out the pre-flight inspection, check that the documentation (CofA, ARC, insurance…) is on board and valid, and record any defect in the technical log.
:::
